claim: In utero exposure to maternal immune activation (MIA) is an environmental risk factor for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: In utero exposure to maternal immune activation (MIA) is an environmental risk factor for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: MIA induced acute upregulation of genes associated with hypoxia, immune signaling, and angiogenesis by 6 hr following exposure.
source: MIA-induced acute upregulation of genes associated with hypoxia, immune signaling, and angiogenesis, by 6 hr following exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data presented in the manuscript showing differential gene expression at E12.5 + 6hr.

claim: Changes in proliferation, neuronal and glial specification, and cortical lamination emerged at E14.5 and peaked at E17.5 following MIA.
source: This acute response was followed by changes in proliferation, neuronal and glial specification, and cortical lamination that emerged at E14.5 and peaked at E17.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course transcriptomic and immunohistochemistry data across developmental stages.

claim: Decreased numbers of proliferative cells in germinal zones were identified in the MIA-exposed cortex.
source: Decreased numbers of proliferative cells in germinal zones and alterations in neuronal and glial populations were identified in the MIA-exposed cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced Ki67+ and PH3+ cells.

claim: Alterations in neuronal and glial populations were identified in the MIA-exposed cortex.
source: Decreased numbers of proliferative cells in germinal zones and alterations in neuronal and glial populations were identified in the MIA-exposed cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing changes in cell type markers.

claim: Epidemiological association between maternal infection and neurodevelopmental disorders has been found for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia (SZ), bipolar disorder (BPD), anxiety, and major depressive disorder (MDD).
source: Epidemiological association between maternal infection and neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) has been found for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia (SZ), bipolar disorder (BPD), anxiety, and major depressive disorder (MDD) (Brown, 2011; Estes and McAllister, 2015; Parboosing et al., 2013; Patterson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Maternal immune activation itself is sufficient to produce NDD-relevant outcomes in offspring in animal models.
source: Indeed, maternal immune activation (MIA) itself is sufficient to produce NDD-relevant outcomes in offspring in animal models (Canetta et al., 2014; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal model studies.

claim: Offspring from female mice exposed to poly(I:C) recapitulate neuropathologies and aberrant behaviors seen in offspring born to flu-infected dams.
source: Offspring from female mice exposed to the toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) agonist and viral mimic polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid [poly(I:C)], and offspring in maternal immune activation models using the bacterial mimic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Depino, 2015; O'Loughlin et al., 2017; Simões et al., 2018), recapitulate neuropathologies and aberrant behaviors seen in offspring born to flu-infected dams (Shi et al., 2003; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative animal model studies.

claim: MIA in mice produces behavioral and cognitive abnormalities with relevance across multiple NDD diagnostic boundaries.
source: MIA in mice produces behavioral and cognitive abnormalities with relevance across multiple NDD diagnostic boundaries (Estes and McAllister, 2016; Malkova et al., 2012; Richetto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies in MIA mouse models.

claim: Poly(I:C) increases proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL1, and TNF-α in the maternal circulation.
source: Poly(I:C) increases proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL1, and TNF-α in the maternal circulation (Ballendine et al., 2015; Dahlgren et al., 2006; Hsiao and Patterson, 2011; Meyer et al., 2006b; Meyer et al., 2006a; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies measuring cytokine levels.

claim: Downstream pathological changes in the brains of offspring have been reported across cell types, from neurons to microglia.
source: Downstream pathological changes in the brains of offspring have been reported across cell types, from neurons to microglia, and these changes have been linked to perturbations in proliferation, migration, and maturation in the developing brain (Haida et al., 2019; Shin Yim et al., 2017; Soumiya et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining cellular changes in MIA offspring.

claim: Recent studies have identified acute transcriptomic changes in fetal brain in mice and rats at single time-points (3–4 hr) following MIA.
source: Recent studies have identified acute transcriptomic changes in fetal brain in mice and rats at single time-points (3–4 hr) following MIA, with significant overlap between transcriptome changes in the cortices of MIA-exposed offspring and those altered in the brains of children with ASD (Lombardo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a transcriptomic study.

claim: There is significant overlap between transcriptome changes in the cortices of MIA-exposed offspring and those altered in the brains of children with ASD.
source: Recent studies have identified acute transcriptomic changes in fetal brain in mice and rats at single time-points (3–4 hr) following MIA, with significant overlap between transcriptome changes in the cortices of MIA-exposed offspring and those altered in the brains of children with ASD (Lombardo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a comparative transcriptomic study.

claim: Induction of MIA via poly(I:C) injection at E12.5 produces relevant phenotypes in mice.
source: Induction of MIA via poly(I:C) injection at E12.5 produces relevant phenotypes in mice (Choi et al., 2016; Shin Yim et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2007) and the specific implementation of this model was recently validated in our hands to produce sufficient levels of MIA to mimic viral infection and cause aberrant behavioral outcomes in offspring (Estes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and validation data from the authors' lab.

claim: The dosage of 30 mg/ml poly(I:C) elicited substantial elevations in maternal serum IL-6 (on average 2200 pg/ml) 4 hr following injection.
source: The dosage of 30 mg/ml poly(I:C) elicited substantial elevations in maternal serum IL-6 (on average 2200 pg/ml) 4 hr following injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA-seq datasets were generated from male and female embryos from 28 independent litters across control and MIA groups.
source: RNA-seq datasets were generated from male and female embryos from 28 independent litters across control and MIA groups, typically with one to three embryos represented per independent litter (Supplementary file 20, Supplementary file 5, File source data 1).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample collection.

claim: For control and MIA, 7 vs. 7 samples at E12.5, 13 vs. 13 samples at E14.5, 6 vs. 6 samples at E17.5, and 10 vs. 12 samples at P0, were compared in a differential expression (DE) analysis.
source: For control and MIA, 7 vs. 7 samples at E12.5, 13 vs. 13 samples at E14.5, 6 vs. 6 samples at E17.5, and 10 vs. 12 samples at P0, were compared in a differential expression (DE) analysis.
evidence: This claim describes the sample sizes used in the analysis.

claim: Developmental age accounts for the majority of variance across samples in principal component analysis.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of MIA and control RNA-seq samples showed developmental age accounts for the majority of variance across samples, with some additional separation between MIA and control groups (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1b-c.

claim: The strongest transcriptional signature was observed at E17.5 (2621 up and 3058 down).
source: The strongest transcriptional signature was observed at E17.5 (2621 up and 3058 down), suggesting dramatic impact of MIA on cortical development at this time-point.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis data.

claim: P0 represented the subtlest transcriptomic signature, with no genes passing the stringent FDR < 0.05 threshold.
source: P0 represented the subtlest transcriptomic signature, with no genes passing the stringent FDR < 0.05 threshold, and with the p < 0.05 DE genes showing a strong upregulation bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis results.

claim: The 82 mouse orthologs of SFARI ASD genes that were expressed at measurable levels were significantly enriched among E17.5 DE genes.
source: The 82 mouse orthologs of SFARI ASD genes that were expressed at measurable levels were significantly enriched among E17.5 DE genes, with 25 upregulated and 19 downregulated DE genes at FDR < 0.05 (p=3.9e-04, hypergeometric test), and 28 upregulated and 28 downregulated DE genes at p < 0.05 (p = 2.8e-06, hypergeometric test) (Figure 1e, Supplementary files 16–17).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Sex-stratified analysis indicated generally concordant DE differences between male and female samples following MIA.
source: Sex-stratified analysis indicated generally concordant DE differences between male and female samples following MIA, although DE effect sizes appeared stronger in females at E14.5 and E17.5, leading to a larger number of DE genes identified independently in females compared to males (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary files 6–15).
evidence: This claim is supported by sex-stratified differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: WGCNA co-expression modules were arbitrarily named after colors, with Grey reserved for genes with no strongly correlated expression patterns.
source: WGCNA co-expression modules were arbitrarily named after colors, with Grey reserved for genes with no strongly correlated expression patterns (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in WGCNA analysis.

claim: The Blue and Turquoise modules represented genes that increased or decreased in expression respectively, during neurodevelopment.
source: The Blue and Turquoise modules represented genes that increased or decreased in expression respectively, during neurodevelopment (Blue: p=9e-34; Turquoise: p=1e-29, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGCNA module analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: There was significant association between genes in Grey (p = 0.007) and Green (p = 0.03) modules and MIA treatment.
source: There was significant association between genes in Grey (p = 0.007) and Green (p = 0.03) modules and MIA treatment, and marginal significance with MIA for the YeMaBl (p = 0.05) module (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of module-trait relationships.

claim: Analysis of the GO BP enrichment of upregulated DE genes in Green and Grey modules identified activation of immune-related pathways, including defense response to virus, as well as angiogenesis and VEGFA signaling.
source: Analysis of the GO BP enrichment of upregulated DE genes in these modules identified activation of immune-related pathways, including defense response to virus, as well as angiogenesis and Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A (VEGFA) signaling (Figures 2c and 3b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figures 2c and 3b.

claim: There were significantly more protein-protein interactions than expected by chance among E12.5 DE (FDR < 0.05) genes (observed edges = 161, expected edges = 46, enrichment = 3.5, STRING p < 1.0e-16).
source: We tested for protein-protein association networks among the acute E12.5 DE (FDR < 0.05) genes using STRING (Szklarczyk et al., 2019), and found significantly more interactions than expected by chance (observed edges = 161, expected edges = 46, enrichment = 3.5, STRING p < 1.0e-16) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by STRING protein-protein interaction network analysis.

claim: Four out of five DE genes tested validated with concordant changes at the protein level as determined by western blot analysis at E17.5.
source: Four out of five DE genes tested validated with concordant changes at the protein level as determined by western blot (WB) analysis at E17.5, showing either statistical significance or trends in the same direction as observed in our transcriptomic analysis (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot validation data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: E17.5 MIA samples exhibited older predicted age values relative to E17.5 saline controls (p = 4.5e-06, T-test).
source: E17.5 MIA samples exhibited older predicted age values relative to E17.5 saline controls (p = 4.5e-06, T-test), and E14.5 MIA samples showed a similar trend (p = 0.07, T-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal modeling analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: GO terms related to proliferation and cell cycle were enriched in the Blue module among downregulated DE genes.
source: GO terms related to proliferation and cell cycle were enriched in the Blue module among downregulated DE genes, and terms related to neuronal differentiation and synapses were enriched in the Turquoise module among upregulated DE genes (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Terms related to neuronal differentiation and synapses were enriched in the Turquoise module among upregulated DE genes.
source: GO terms related to proliferation and cell cycle were enriched in the Blue module among downregulated DE genes, and terms related to neuronal differentiation and synapses were enriched in the Turquoise module among upregulated DE genes (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: PAX6+, SOX9+ and SOX2+ cell distribution patterns showed that progenitors localized correctly around the cortical ventricular zone in coronal brain sections.
source: PAX6+, SOX9+ and SOX2+ cell distribution patterns showed that progenitors localized correctly around the cortical ventricular zone in coronal brain sections; all analyzed cell populations were significantly reduced in MIA brains compared to controls (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4e-f.

claim: All analyzed progenitor cell populations were significantly reduced in MIA brains compared to controls.
source: PAX6+, SOX9+ and SOX2+ cell distribution patterns showed that progenitors localized correctly around the cortical ventricular zone in coronal brain sections; all analyzed cell populations were significantly reduced in MIA brains compared to controls (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4e-f.

claim: MIA brains showed a decrease in SOX9+ cells in the ventricular zone (SOX9 VZ, p=0.0198).
source: MIA brains showed a decrease in SOX9+ cells in the ventricular zone (VZ), which is expressed in progenitors (Scott et al., 2010). We also observed increased SOX9+ cells above the VZ in the neocortex, which can remain expressed in a subset of cells, including oligodendrocyte progenitors and maturing astrocytes (Klum et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2017) (SOX9 VZ, p=0.0198; nCtx, p=0.0058, two tailed Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data.

claim: Increased SOX9+ cells were observed above the VZ in the neocortex in MIA brains (nCtx, p=0.0058).
source: We also observed increased SOX9+ cells above the VZ in the neocortex, which can remain expressed in a subset of cells, including oligodendrocyte progenitors and maturing astrocytes (Klum et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2017) (SOX9 VZ, p=0.0198; nCtx, p=0.0058, two tailed Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data and citations to literature on SOX9 expression.

claim: Reduced expression of SOX2, a progenitor marker that is restricted to the VZ, was observed in MIA brains (SOX2 VZ, p=0.0006).
source: Reduced expression of SOX2, a progenitor marker that is restricted to the VZ, was also observed in MIA brains (SOX2 VZ, p=0.0006 two tailed Student's t-test) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Quantification of Ki67+ cells and PH3+ cells in the neocortex confirmed the MIA-induced reduction in progenitor and mitotic populations at E17.5 (Ki67, p=0.0198; PH3, p=0.0003).
source: Quantification of Ki67+ cells and PH3+ cells in the neocortex confirmed the MIA-induced reduction in progenitor and mitotic populations at E17.5 (Ki67, p=0.0198; PH3, p=0.0003, two tailed Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data.

claim: Ki67/PH3 ratios indicated a reduced proportion of progenitor cells in M phase in MIA brains at E17.5 (p=0.0005 Chi-squared).
source: The ratio of PH3+ (mitosis) cells to Ki67+ (all stages of cell division) cells was then used to determine whether cell cycle kinetics or the number of actively dividing cells in M phase was different in the MIA-exposed group. Ki67/PH3 ratios indicated a reduced proportion of progenitor cells in M phase in MIA brains at this specific time-point (p=0.0005 Chi-squared) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: MIA has been associated with altered cortical thickness and reported to cause cortical dysplasia in young adult MIA offspring.
source: MIA has been associated with altered cortical thickness and reported to cause cortical dysplasia in young adult MIA offspring (Smith et al., 2007; Soumiya et al., 2011; Tsukada et al., 2015), with stereotypic dysplasia impacting lamination localized to the somatosensory cortex reported in one MIA model (Choi et al., 2016; Shin Yim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All control brains showed lamination overlap between TBR1/CTIP2 layers, while absence of TBR1/CTIP2 lamination overlap was observed in four out of six analyzed MIA brains at E17.5.
source: Brains from three MIA litters and two control litters were co-stained with TBR1 and CTIP2 cortical markers (as shown in a-b) and analyzed for lamination overlap occurrence (n = 4 control, n = 6 MIA). While all control brains showed lamination overlap between TBR1/CTIP2 layers, absence of TBR1/CTIP2 lamination overlap was observed in four out of six analyzed MIA brains.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry analysis of cortical lamination.

claim: The number of TBR1+ and CTIP2+ cells, but not SATB2+ cells, were significantly reduced in the neocortex from MIA offspring (TBR1+ cells, p=0.0138; CTIP2+ cells, p=0.0119; SATB2+ cells, p=0.306).
source: The number of TBR1+ and CTIP2+ cells, but not SATB2+ cells, were also significantly reduced in the neocortex from MIA offspring (TBR1+ cells, p=0.0138; CTIP2+ cells, p=0.0119; SATB2+ cells, p=0.306, two tailed Student t-test) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5e.

claim: A significant reduction in CTIP2 layer thickness and a similar trend in TBR1 layer thickness were found in the MIA brains.
source: We found a significant reduction in CTIP2 layer thickness and a similar trend in TBR1 layer thickness in the MIA brains. In contrast, SATB2 showed an MIA-induced significant increase in layer thickness with no change in the more external layer represented by CUX1 (TBR1 thickness, p=0.081; CTIP2 thickness, 0.024; SATB2 thickness, p=0.039; CUX1, p=0.430, two tailed Student's t-test). (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by layer thickness measurements shown in Figure 5f.

claim: SATB2 showed an MIA-induced significant increase in layer thickness (p=0.039).
source: In contrast, SATB2 showed an MIA-induced significant increase in layer thickness with no change in the more external layer represented by CUX1 (TBR1 thickness, p=0.081; CTIP2 thickness, 0.024; SATB2 thickness, p=0.039; CUX1, p=0.430, two tailed Student's t-test). (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by layer thickness measurements shown in Figure 5f.

claim: No obvious cortical dysplasia or gross alterations in brain anatomy were found in the analyzed rostral and caudal regions at E17.5.
source: In contrast to previous reports (Choi et al., 2016), we did not find obvious cortical dysplasia or gross alterations in brain anatomy in the analyzed rostral and caudal regions, including somatosensory cortex and S1DZ (Figure 5e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by gross anatomical analysis shown in Figure 5e-f.

claim: The number of cells expressing GFAP was increased in MIA offspring, mapping specifically to cells that seemed to emerge ventral from the neocortical VZ.
source: Concordant with RNA-seq results, the number of cells expressing GFAP, a protein found in radial glia and a subset of astrocytes (Eng et al., 2000), was increased in MIA offspring, mapping specifically to cells that seemed to emerge ventral from the neocortical VZ (Figure 6a–b,q, Figure 4—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6a-b,q.

claim: OLIG2+ cells were increased in MIA brains compared to controls (n = 3 per group, p=0.0134).
source: OLIG2, which is expressed in oligodendrocyte progenitors and mature cells as well as transiently in astrocyte progenitors (Dimou et al., 2008), was also upregulated at E17.5 in the MIA group. OLIG2+ cells were increased in MIA brains compared to controls (n = 3 per group, p=0.0134, Student's t-test) (Figure 6c–d,k, Figure 4—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 6c-d,k.

claim: PDGFRα was increased in MIA brains compared to controls (n = 7 per group, zone 1 p<0.0001, zone 2 p=0.0063, zone 3 p=0.0125).
source: PDGFRα, a marker of early developing oligodendrocytes, was also increased in MIA brains compared to controls (n = 7 per group, zone 1 p<0.0001, zone 2 p=0.0063, zone 3 p=0.0125, Student's t-test) (Figure 6e–f,l).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 6e-f,l.

claim: The number of cells positive for DLX2 protein in the neocortex were comparable when assessed via IHC in the MIA and control groups (n = 3 per group, total DLX2 p=0.5494).
source: Although Dlx2 expression was downregulated in the MIA group from bulk tissue dissections at E17.5, the number of cells positive for DLX2 protein in the neocortex were comparable when assessed via IHC in the MIA and control groups (n = 3 per group, total DLX2 p=0.5494; by zones DLX2, zone 1 P=0.9848, zone 2 P=0.6903, zone 3 P=0.2714, Student's t-test) (Figure 6g–h and m,o).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 6g-h and m,o.

claim: GAD protein in the DLX2+ subpopulation was increased across the neocortex of MIA brains (n = 3 per group, total DLX2+/GAD67 p=0.0004).
source: In contrast, GAD protein in this DLX2+ subpopulation, assessed by the pan-GABAergic marker GAD67+, was increased across the neocortex of MIA brains, and was not restricted to any specific zones of the neocortex (n = 3 per group, total DLX2+/GAD67 p=0.0004; by zones DLX2+/GAD67, zone 1 P=0.2277, zone 2 P=0.1352, zone 3 P=0.2862, Student's t-test) (Figure 6i–j and n,p).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 6i-j and n,p.

claim: MIA-associated transcriptional signatures were robust, changed greatly across the surveyed time-points, and revealed novel pathways and processes involved in pathology.
source: MIA-associated transcriptional signatures were robust, changed greatly across the surveyed time- points, and revealed novel pathways and processes involved in pathology.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Among MIA-associated DE up-regulated and down-regulated genes, there was strong enrichment for ASD-relevant loci.
source: Among MIA-associated DE up-regulated and down-regulated genes, there was strong enrichment for ASD-relevant loci, indicating the general translational relevance of our MIA model to ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis of SFARI genes.

claim: Both male and female samples were examined, and we did not find evidence for strong sex-specific DE signatures or impacts on neuroanatomy.
source: Both male and female samples were examined, and we did not find evidence for strong sex-specific DE signatures or impacts on neuroanatomy.
evidence: This claim is based on sex-stratified analysis showing concordant results between sexes.

claim: There is overlap in the acute induction signatures identified here and acute changes reported in other mid-gestational MIA models.
source: There is overlap in the acute induction signatures identified here and acute changes reported in other mid-gestational MIA models, including those using a range of injection gestational ages and rat models of LPS (Carpentier et al., 2013; Meyer, 2014; Meyer et al., 2006a; O'Loughlin et al., 2017; Richetto et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited literature.

claim: Previous studies linked maternal immune challenge, prenatal brain hypoxia, and impacts on proliferation, neurogenesis, and cortical lamination.
source: Previous studies linked maternal immune challenge, prenatal brain hypoxia, and impacts on proliferation (Stolp et al., 2011), neurogenesis, and cortical lamination (Carpentier et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Induction of hypoxia, cellular metabolism and neuroimmune transcriptional signatures persist at reduced levels at least through P0.
source: Notably, induction of hypoxia, cellular metabolism and neuroimmune transcriptional signatures, particularly captured here by the Green module, persist at reduced levels at least through P0, and may indicate lasting perturbation to these pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of module expression trajectories across time points.

claim: Vegfa was upregulated in MIA-exposed animals at all time-points and was among the strongest DE genes at E12.5 and P0.
source: Vegfa was upregulated in MIA-exposed animal at all time-points and was among the strongest DE genes at E12.5 and P0.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis across time points.

claim: Vegfa is critical for cortical development promoting neurogenesis and neurite outgrowth, as well as angiogenesis.
source: Vegfa is critical for cortical development promoting neurogenesis and neurite outgrowth, as well as angiogenesis (Bayless et al., 2016; Mackenzie and Ruhrberg, 2012; Rosenstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on Vegfa function.

claim: Upregulation of Vegfa is found in several NDDs and psychiatric disorders, including SZ and depression.
source: Upregulation of Vegfa is found in several NDDs and psychiatric disorders, including SZ and depression, and was also reported in a different MIA mouse model (Arrode-Brusés and Brusés, 2012; Hohman et al., 2015; Iga et al., 2007; Isung et al., 2012; Kahl et al., 2009; Lee and Kim, 2012; Lizano et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical and animal model studies.

claim: Induction of angiogenesis in the developing cortex independently causes a transition from proliferative state to neuronal maturation.
source: Induction of angiogenesis in the developing cortex also independently causes a transition from proliferative state to neuronal maturation (Bayless et al., 2016; Javaherian and Kriegstein, 2009; Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on angiogenesis and neuronal development.

claim: At six hours after MIA, there is a shift in expression of differentiation and neuronal maturation processes to increased proliferative processes.
source: Initially, at six hours after MIA, there is a shift in expression of differentiation and neuronal maturation processes (e.g. synaptogenesis) to increased proliferative processes (e.g. positive regulation of cell cycle).
evidence: This claim is based on gene ontology analysis of E12.5 differential expression.

claim: MIA induces an acute expenditure of the neocortical progenitor pools, which leads to an expedited maturation of cells that would normally be generated later during development.
source: At this developmental stage, our data suggest that MIA induces an acute expenditure of the neocortical, and potentially other, progenitor pools, which in turn leads to an expedited maturation of cells that would normally be generated later during development.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of findings across time points.

claim: By E17.5, multiple progenitor and cell cycle markers were significantly decreased in the MIA brains while concordantly, an increase in maturational markers and laminar position that resembled a more developed cortex was observed.
source: Specifically, by E17.5, multiple progenitor and cell cycle markers were significantly decreased in the MIA brains while concordantly, we observed an increase in maturational markers and laminar position that resembled a more developed cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic and immunohistochemistry data at E17.5.

claim: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, GABAergic interneurons and radially migrating excitatory neuron precursors were affected by MIA.
source: Finally, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, GABAergic interneurons and radially migrating excitatory neuron precursors were effected, suggesting an unbiased impact on progenitors of multiple brain cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry analysis of multiple cell types.

claim: The findings of disrupted cortical lamination following the acute MIA signature are consistent with, but not identical to previous studies showing cortical dysplasia associated with MIA-induced aberrant behavior in offspring.
source: Our findings of disrupted cortical lamination following the acute MIA signature are consistent with, but not identical to previous studies showing cortical dysplasia associated with MIA-induced aberrant behavior in offspring (Choi et al., 2016; Shin Yim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares current findings to cited previous studies.

claim: Perturbation to neuronal migration, potentially due to differences in an early exit of pyramidal neuron precursors from the cell cycle, contributes to MIA-associated lamination differences identified at E17.5.
source: Our findings suggest that perturbation to neuronal migration, potentially due to differences in an early exit of pyramidal neuron precursors from the cell cycle that led to cells further along in their radial migration/lamination, developmental progression, at least in part contribute to MIA-associated lamination differences identified at E17.5 here.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the pattern of findings.

claim: By P0, MIA-associated transcriptional signatures were reduced, which suggests a transient or attenuating effect on cortical patterning.
source: By P0, these signatures were reduced, which suggests a transient or attenuating effect on cortical patterning.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of differential expression across time points.

claim: The subtle changes in gene expression at P0 are consistent with deficits in synapse formation that require changes in expression of immune molecules in neurons from newborn MIA offspring.
source: Nonetheless, the subtle changes in gene expression at P0 are consistent with deficits in synapse formation that require changes in expression of immune molecules in neurons from newborn MIA offspring (Elmer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim connects current findings to cited previous work on synaptic deficits.

claim: Atypical neurodevelopmental gene expression networks have been reported in a cortical neurodevelopmental model using autism-patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Consistent with links between NDDs and developmental timing, atypical neurodevelopmental gene expression networks have been reported in a cortical neurodevelopmental model using autism-patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (Bayless et al., 2016; Schafer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using patient-derived cells.

claim: The majority of the ASD-relevant genes that were DE following MIA were associated with perturbation to the modules associated with neurodevelopmental processes.
source: The majority of the ASD-relevant genes that were DE following MIA (Figure 1e) were associated with perturbation to the modules associated with neurodevelopmental processes.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of SFARI gene enrichment in WGCNA modules.

claim: Some aspects of the transition from neurogenesis to astrogenesis appear to occur at an earlier stage following MIA.
source: Our findings suggest some aspects of the transition from neurogenesis to astrogenesis appear to occur at an earlier stage following MIA based on similar signatures of SOX9+ and GFAP+ cells reported in literature (Bansod et al., 2017), and increased OLIG2+ cells and more mature GAD67+ DLX2+ interneurons in the cortex following MIA.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on cell type marker analysis and comparison to literature.

claim: MIA drives acute and lasting transcriptional changes that impact specific cell populations during forebrain development.
source: Altogether, our analyses indicate that MIA drives acute and lasting transcriptional changes that impact specific cell populations during forebrain development, disrupting normal developmental timing and causing increased numbers of astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and altered molecular properties of GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: The timing of MIA during gestation is known to cause a range of phenotypes in offspring.
source: The timing of MIA during gestation is known to cause a range of phenotypes in offspring, and thus the findings here regarding mid-gestational MIA at E12.5 may not generalize to other models with different timing of MIA induction, especially for later gestational MIA after neurogenesis is largely complete.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge of MIA models and acknowledges limitations.

claim: The strong embryonic signatures observed were generally consistent across sexes.
source: Further, the strong embryonic signatures we observe were generally consistent across sexes, raising the question of whether secondary insults or sex-specific protective effects contribute to some reports of sex differences in pathology following MIA (Haida et al., 2019; Naviaux et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on sex-stratified analysis and raises questions about sex differences reported in other studies.

claim: The overlapping results between this study and published single time-point studies of the acute MIA fetal brain transcriptional response suggest some consistency across bacterial and viral mimics, and rat and mouse models.
source: Nonetheless, the overlapping results between our study and published single time-point studies of the acute MIA fetal brain transcriptional response suggest some consistency across bacterial and viral mimics, and rat and mouse models.
evidence: This claim compares current findings to previous literature to suggest generalizability.

claim: Injection of poly(I:C) at E12.5 consistently elevates serum IL-6 in dams 4 hr following injection, compared with little response in dams injected with saline.
source: Injection of poly(I:C) at E12.5 consistently elevates serum IL-6 in dams 4 hr following injection, compared with little response in dams injected with saline.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice utilized in this study harbor Segmented Filamentous Bacteria (SFB).
source: Mice utilized in this study do harbor Segmented Filamentous Bacteria (SFB) (Estes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation.

claim: Virgin females in the lowest 25th percentile of immune responsiveness to poly(I:C) (IL-6 serum levels) were excluded from the study to reduce variability and ensure sufficient immune responsiveness of all included dams.
source: Since female mice display a wide range of baseline immunoreactivity to poly(I:C) that dictates susceptibility and resilience of offspring from later pregnancies to MIA, virgin females in the lowest 25th percentile of immune responsiveness to poly(I:C) (IL-6 serum levels) were excluded from the study to reduce variability and ensure sufficient immune responsiveness of all included dams.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the experimental design.
